description: Master psychophysical measurement: absolute thresholds, difference thresholds and Weber's law, Fechner's logarithmic scaling, signal detection theory (hits, misses, false alarms), and sensory adaptation.

slides.title: Welcome to Psychophysics
slides.content:
# Thresholds & Signal Detection Theory

How faint a sound can human ears detect? How much sugar must be dissolved in a cup of coffee before you notice a change in sweetness?

These questions form the core of **Psychophysics** - the foundational branch of psychology founded by Gustav Fechner in 1860 that studies the quantitative relationships between physical stimulus intensities and subjective psychological sensations.

## In This Module, You Will Learn:
- The Absolute Threshold and classic sensory detection baselines
- The Difference Threshold (Just Noticeable Difference) and Weber's Law
- Signal Detection Theory (SDT) and decision-making criteria
- The biological mechanics and survival advantages of Sensory Adaptation

slides.title: The Absolute Threshold
slides.content:
# The Absolute Threshold

## Definition:
- The **Absolute Threshold** is the minimum physical stimulus intensity required for an organism to detect a stimulus **50% of the time**.

## Why 50% of the Time?
- Human sensory detection is not an all-or-none switch. Due to background neural noise, momentary fluctuations in attention, and metabolic fatigue, detection exists along an S-shaped psychometric curve.
- A stimulus exactly at the absolute threshold is detected on half of the experimental trials and missed on the other half.

slides.title: Classic Human Sensory Absolute Thresholds
slides.content:
# Human Absolute Thresholds Under Ideal Conditions

Under pristine laboratory conditions with zero background noise, human sensory receptors display extraordinary sensitivity (Galanter, 1962):

| Sensory Modality | Established Absolute Threshold Benchmark |
|---|---|
| **Vision** | A single candle flame seen from 30 miles away on a clear, pitch-black night |
| **Audition** | The ticking of a mechanical watch from 20 feet away in a completely quiet room |
| **Taste** | One teaspoon of sugar dissolved in two gallons of water |
| **Smell** | One drop of perfume diffused throughout a three-room apartment |
| **Touch** | The wing of a bee falling onto your cheek from a distance of 1 centimeter |

slides.title: Absolute Threshold Check
slides.content: Assess your understanding of the absolute threshold definition!
slides.quizQuestion: In psychophysics, what is the exact operational definition of an Absolute Threshold?
quizOptions: The maximum stimulus intensity that human sensory receptors can tolerate without pain
The minimum stimulus intensity detected by an observer exactly 50% of the time
The point at which sensory adaptation permanently halts neural firing
The intensity required for 100% flawless detection on every single trial

slides.title: The Difference Threshold (JND)
slides.content:
# The Difference Threshold (JND)

## Definition:
- The **Difference Threshold**, also known as the **Just Noticeable Difference (JND)**, is the minimum physical difference between two stimuli required for an observer to detect a difference **50% of the time**.

## The Concept:
- If you hold a 100-gram weight in your hand, adding a single grain of sand (0.01 grams) is undetectable.
- You must add a specific minimal amount of additional weight before your somatosensory cortex detects that the object has become heavier.
- This minimal required change is the JND.

slides.title: Weber's Law: Constant Proportions
slides.content:
# Weber's Law: Constant Proportions

German physiologist **Ernst Weber** made a profound discovery: *The size of the Just Noticeable Difference is not a constant absolute amount, but a constant proportion of the initial stimulus intensity!*

## The Mathematical Principle:
```
Change in Intensity (Delta I) / Original Intensity (I) = Constant (k)
```

- If the Weber constant (**k**) for weight is 2% (0.02):
  - For a 100-gram weight, you need to add **2 grams** to notice a difference.
  - For a 1,000-gram weight, adding 2 grams is completely imperceptible! You must add **20 grams** to detect a difference!
- **Key Takeaway:** As stimulus intensity increases, the amount of change needed to detect a difference increases proportionally.

slides.title: Weber Fractions Across Senses
slides.content:
# Weber Constants Across Sensory Modalities

Different human sensory systems exhibit distinct Weber fractions (**k**), reflecting their evolutionary sensitivity:

| Modality | Physical Stimulus Dimension | Weber Fraction (k) |
|---|---|---|
| **Electric Shock** | Electrical current across skin | approx 0.01 (1%) - extremely sensitive |
| **Light** | Visual brightness intensity | approx 0.08 (8%) |
| **Weight** | Lifted somatic weight | approx 0.02 (2%) |
| **Sound** | Auditory frequency / pitch | approx 0.003 (0.3%) |
| **Sound** | Auditory loudness / intensity | approx 0.05 (5%) |
| **Taste** | Saltiness concentration in water | approx 0.20 (20%) - least sensitive |

slides.title: Fechner's Law: Logarithmic Sensation
slides.content:
# Fechner's Law: Scaling the Mind

Building upon Weber's work, **Gustav Fechner** formulated the first mathematical law of cognitive psychology (**Fechner's Law**):

```
Subjective Psychological Sensation (S) = k x log(Physical Stimulus Intensity)
```

## The Logarithmic Reality:
- Physical intensity must increase exponentially for subjective psychological sensation to increase linearly in arithmetic steps!
- To double the perceived brightness of a room, you cannot merely double the number of lightbulbs; you must increase light intensity tenfold.
- (This logarithmic scaling protects our sensory systems from being instantly overwhelmed by the vast physical ranges found in nature).

slides.title: Signal Detection Theory (SDT): Overview
slides.content:
# Signal Detection Theory (SDT)

Traditional psychophysics assumed that sensory thresholds were fixed biological constants. In the 1960s, **Signal Detection Theory (SDT)** revolutionized psychology by recognizing that detection is NOT purely sensory:

> *Detecting a stimulus depends on both the physical intensity of the signal AND the observer's psychological decision criterion, motivation, expectation, and fatigue!*

## The Two Realities:
In any detection task (e.g., a radiologist scanning a mammogram for tumor signals, or an air traffic controller watching a radar screen), there are two components:
1. **Signal:** The target stimulus being searched for.
2. **Noise:** All background interference (environmental noise, machine static, and internal random firing in the nervous system).

slides.title: The Four SDT Outcomes Matrix
slides.content:
# The Signal Detection Matrix

Every signal detection trial produces one of **Four Discrete Outcomes** based on the presence of the signal and the observer's decision:

```
                                    TRUE PHYSICAL STATE
                            Signal Present       |       Signal Absent
                       +-------------------------+-------------------------+
DECISION:              |           HIT           |       FALSE ALARM       |
'YES, Signal Detected' | (Correct Detection)     | (False Positive)        |
                       +-------------------------+-------------------------+
DECISION:              |          MISS           |    CORRECT REJECTION    |
'NO, Signal Not Seen'  | (False Negative)        | (True Negative)         |
                       +-------------------------+-------------------------+
```

- **Hit:** Signal is present, and observer says 'YES'.
- **Miss:** Signal is present, and observer says 'NO'.
- **False Alarm:** Signal is absent, and observer says 'YES'.
- **Correct Rejection:** Signal is absent, and observer says 'NO'.

slides.content: Verify your comprehension of the four Signal Detection Theory outcomes!

slides.title: Sensitivity (d') and Response Bias (beta)
slides.content:
# Sensitivity (d') vs. Response Bias (beta)

Signal Detection Theory mathematically separates two distinct psychological dimensions:

## 1. Perceptual Sensitivity (d-prime / d'):
- The observer's true sensory capacity to distinguish signals from background noise.
- Determined by physiological hardware (e.g., quality of eyes, clarity of radar screen).
- If a person has sharp vision and good equipment, **d'** is high; if vision is degraded by cataracts, **d'** is low.

## 2. Response Bias / Criterion (beta / c):
- The observer's subjective decision strategy or willingness to say 'YES' under uncertainty, driven by payoffs and penalties:
  - **Liberal Criterion:** Says 'YES' frequently; maximizes Hits, but suffers many False Alarms (e.g., radiologist looking for cancer - missing a tumor is fatal, so they flag any suspicious shadow).
  - **Conservative Criterion:** Says 'YES' only when 100% certain; minimizes False Alarms, but suffers many Misses (e.g., jury declaring a defendant guilty).

slides.title: Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC)
slides.content:
# The ROC Curve: Mapping Performance

In Signal Detection Theory, an observer's performance across varying criteria is plotted as a **Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve**:

```
  1.0 +                 .*   (High Sensitivity d' = 3.0)
      |              .*
      |           .*
HIT   |        .*
RATE  |     .*
      |  .*                  (Low Sensitivity d' = 1.0)
      |.*-----------------   (Zero Sensitivity d' = 0: Pure Chance)
  0.0 +-------------------+
     0.0      FALSE ALARM RATE      1.0
```

- **The Diagonal Line (d' = 0):** Pure chance guessing (Hit rate equals False Alarm rate).
- **Bowed Curve:** The further the curve bows toward the top-left corner (100% Hits, 0% False Alarms), the higher the observer's true sensory sensitivity **d'**.

slides.title: Sensory Adaptation: Mechanics & Purpose
slides.content:
# Sensory Adaptation: Tuning Out Constancy

## Definition:
- **Sensory Adaptation** is the diminishing sensitivity of sensory receptors to constant, unchanging environmental stimulation over time.

## Real-World Examples:
- Stepping into a heavily chlorinated swimming pool: it feels freezing at first, but feels comfortably warm after 5 minutes.
- Putting on a wristwatch or wool sweater: you feel the fabric pressing on your skin initially, but within seconds you completely lose conscious awareness of it.
- Entering a friend's apartment: you immediately smell their pet cat, but they smell nothing because their olfactory receptors have adapted.

## Cellular Mechanism:
- Prolonged static stimulation causes sensory receptor cells to decrease their action potential firing rates.

slides.quizQuestion: Why do our eyes not undergo complete sensory adaptation to static images in everyday life, which would cause an unmoving visual scene to completely vanish from sight?
quizOptions: Rods and cones do not contain photopigments
The eyes constantly execute microscopic involuntary tremors called microsaccades that continuously shift light across fresh photoreceptors
Visual signals bypass the thalamus entirely
The lens constantly flips upside down

slides.title: Why Don't Our Eyes Adapt? Microsaccades
slides.content:
# Visual Adaptation & Microsaccades

If sensory receptors adapt to static stimulation, *why doesn't an unmoving page of text fade into gray while you stare at it?*

## The Biological Solution: Microsaccades
- Even when you stare fixedly at a single point, your eyes execute involuntary, microscopic tremors and rapid drift movements called **Microsaccades** several times per second.
- These tiny vibrations ensure that the visual image on the retina is constantly shifting across new, unfatigued rods and cones!

## The Stabilized Retinal Image Experiment (Riggs, 1953):
- Researchers attached tiny mirrors onto contact lenses, causing visual images to move in exact synchrony with eye tremors (stabilizing the image on the exact same photoreceptors).
- **The Result:** Within 3 seconds, the image began to fracture and vanished completely into blank gray! The moment the image was jiggled, it reappeared instantly!

slides.title: Evolutionary Advantages of Adaptation
slides.content:
# The Evolutionary Genius of Sensory Adaptation

Why did natural selection engineer sensory adaptation into virtually every living animal?

## The Survival Rationale:
- The sensory environment contains infinite sensory noise (the hum of air conditioning, the pressure of your shoes, the ambient temperature).
- If our brains processed all static inputs with equal intensity, conscious cognitive processing would instantly crash from sensory overload.
- **Adaptation frees up cognitive bandwidth:** It silences static, predictable background noise so the nervous system can stay laser-focused on **novelty and change** (which usually signal food, mating opportunities, or predators!).

slides.title: Course 5 Summary & Sensory Synthesis
slides.content:
# Course 5 Summary: Sensation & Perception

## Master Curriculum Reviewed:
- **Vision:** Eye anatomy (cornea, pupil, lens accommodation, retina), rods vs. cones, foveal acuity, visual pathway (optic chiasm to V1 feature detectors), dual streams (Ventral 'WHAT' vs. Dorsal 'WHERE/HOW'), trichromatic & opponent-process color synthesis, and binocular/monocular depth cues.
- **Hearing & Non-Visual Senses:** Auditory mechanics (eardrum, ossicles, cochlear basilar membrane hair cells), pitch perception (Place Theory + Frequency/Volley Principle), gustation (5 tastes), olfaction (direct limbic projection), cutaneous touch, Gate-Control Theory of pain, and vestibular balance.
- **Perceptual Processes:** Bottom-up (data-driven) vs. top-down (concept-driven), Gestalt organization (figure-ground, closure, proximity), perceptual constancies (size, shape, color), and inattentional/change blindness.
- **Thresholds & Psychophysics:** Absolute threshold (detected 50% of the time), Difference threshold / JND, Weber's Law (Delta I / I = k), Fechner's logarithmic scaling, Signal Detection Theory (Hits, Misses, False Alarms, Correct Rejections; d' sensitivity vs. beta response bias), and Sensory Adaptation (microsaccades).

> **Congratulations!** You have completed all learning modules for **Sensation & Perception**. Next, we enter **States of Consciousness** to explore sleep, dreams, hypnosis, drugs, and awareness!
